articles.summary: ASML Vs. Taiwan Semiconductor: Who Can More Fully Satisfy AI Demand?  24/7 Wall St.
articles.full_text:
Both ASML and TSMC say AI demand outstrips everything they can build, but each company is betting on a different strategy to close that gap. One controls the scarcest tool in chipmaking while the other controls the fabs, the nodes,…
ASML (NASDAQ:ASML | ASML Price Prediction) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) reported third-quarter results a day apart. Both said the same thing: AI demand is bigger than what they can build. ASML makes the EUV machines, and TSMC runs them to print 2nm and 3nm chips. For anyone looking at picks-and-shovels plays beyond the chipmakers themselves (we examined seven of the power, cooling, and networking suppliers behind the data-center expansion in a free report), the question is which one can close its supply gap faster.
Upgrades Lift ASML While 2nm Squeezes TSMC
ASML posted revenue of $13.06B, up 55.2% YoY. That kind of growth tells you chipmakers are buying tools as fast as ASML can ship them. EPS of $14.48 came in well above the $10.66 consensus, though a $570.65M one-time investment gain flatters that number. The cleaner signal was Installed Base Management, which reached €3.3 billion, above guidance. The CFO explained why: “The ability to enable an increase in capacity through upgrades on the same footprint is very compelling for our customers.”
TSMC earned $4.60 per ADR, beating the $4.46 estimate. High-performance computing (HPC) made up 68% of revenue, which shows how far AI has reshaped the customer base. Gross margin fell to 66.4% because 2nm, now at 8% of wafer revenue, still costs more to make than it earns back. Scaling up a new node quickly comes at that price.
| Business Driver | ASML | TSMC | 
|---|---|---|
| Main Growth Engine | Memory system sales seen up around 75% in 2026 | AI wafers on 2nm and 3nm | 
| Capacity Lever | Faster NXE:3800F at 260 wafers per hour | N2 capacity set to more than double in 2027 | 
| Margin Risk | Costs of scaling up production and suppliers | Overseas fab dilution growing to 3%–4% | 
ASML Charges for Scarcity While TSMC Builds Through It
ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet admitted that planned 2027 and 2028 supply “will not fully meet the demand of our customers.” Customers already want slots for 2029 and even 2030. ASML has finished price-increase talks on its most critical tools, with the full effect landing from 2028 onward. Being sold out gives ASML pricing power.
TSMC is spending its way toward more supply instead. CEO C.C. Wei said “the gap between demand and supply is still quite big.” The company is keeping 2026 capex at $60 billion to $64 billion with nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress. It also plans to wait on High NA EUV until 2030, once the tool costs make sense for mass production.
ASML’s 2028 Capacity Number Is the Catalyst to Watch
ASML’s Capital Markets Day on June 10, 2027 should reveal whether it plans expansion beyond the 30% increase. China, at around 20% of total net sales, leaves ASML exposed to export controls. For TSMC, watch Arizona’s second fab starting volume production in the third quarter of 2027 and its lack of back-end packaging capacity.
Why I Lean Toward TSMC to Close the Gap
ASML is the tighter chokepoint, but TSMC controls more of the ways to add output: fabs, node transitions and advanced packaging. TSMC also trades near 21 times forward earnings, compared with ASML’s 29. That gap means investors pay a lower multiple of forward earnings for TSMC’s AI production exposure than for ASML’s. A much larger 2028 ramp from ASML would shift that comparison.

articles.full_text:
Infinity Ward recently opened its Krakow research and development centre to us to showcase the technical advancements powering Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Infinity Ward Poland studio head Michal Drobot was on hand to present debug footage that explained how current-gen hardware on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and PC enables unprecedented visual and systemic upgrades. While a Nintendo Switch 2 version is also launching in parallel via Digital Legends, the core engine focus remains firmly on pushing broader performance and graphical boundaries - including ray-marched smoke and fog, revamped rasterisation techniques informed by path tracing, and a comprehensively reworked animation and movement system.
Let's start with one of the standout additions, a brand new volumetric ray-marched smoke and fog system built exclusively for MW4. Working in tandem with traditional transparencies, this voxel-based solution allows players to interact directly with smoke plumes using gunfire or vehicles. Bullets carve precise temporary holes through the volume - as in Counter-Strike 2 - while sprinting characters displace wisps naturally, all operating within a fixed GPU performance ceiling.
This unified voxel framework extends seamlessly across atmospheric elements, height fog, and overhead clouds, ensuring consistent competitive balance across all online multiplayer and DMZ modes. Server and local client synchronisation guarantees that visual interactions such as lighting, shadows, and smoke dispersion appear identically for every participant. Furthermore, volumetric fog self shadows and interacts dynamically with animated light sources within the environment.
Weather systems also benefit heavily from the new voxel architecture, supporting dynamic transitions between sunshine, rainfall and snow across expansive open maps - a huge change for open-ended modes like DMZ. Snow layers accumulate dynamically on top of existing level geometry, allowing players to gradually reveal the original terrain beneath. Additionally, expanded character and object voxels now track more environmental states than previous games - a great range of variables that coats soldiers in mud, dust, blood or water streaks depending on their movement.
Next there's the new material workflow used in Modern Warfare 4. While full path tracing is reserved for internal visual reference only due to its heavy performance cost - and RT global illumination and RT reflections are PC-exclusive features - MW4 developers chose to heavily optimise rasterisation pipelines, achieving visual results remarkably close to path tracing at a fraction of the computational expense. This strategy ensures the game easily maintains a high frame-rate across a much wider spectrum of hardware, a key consideration given how much of Call of Duty's audience plays on console with 60fps in mind.
A core component of this improved rasterised approach is the neural light grid, which leverages machine learning compression to handle dynamic ambient occlusion and global illumination, a rethought approach that seeks to avoid the typical artefacts caused by screen-space reflections (SSR) and screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO). By storing lighting data more efficiently, light probes can be distributed sparsely across levels without sacrificing visual fidelity. Incidentally, it's an innovation that also helps to reduce the game's installation sizes alongside improved texture streaming techniques.
In part, material rendering receives a major upgrade through custom capture hardware known as the ATVI CT Reflectometer 2.0. By capturing physical surface properties across multiple light gradients, artists are able to access accurate bidirectional reflectance distribution function values for skin, clothing and metallic surfaces. This new material workflow integrates well with the enhanced rasterised ambient occlusion and global illumination passes.
Under the hood, significant optimisations target the entire rendering pipeline through advanced variable rate shading. Variable rate shading dynamically compresses visual data in less critical areas while preserving full native resolution where it matters most, drastically reducing overall graphical overhead - and this time, it's now applied throughout the entire render pipeline, not just for the final rendered pixels. Additional efficiency is gained through multi-resolution transparencies, with effects like smoke scaling in resolution based on distance.
Supporting these techniques, a hybrid rendering setup is also in place: combining traditional forward rendering (F+) with a visibility buffer (V+) for dense geometry. Where it's efficient to do so, parts of the scene will flip from one to the other, with F+ tending to handle triangles nearer the player.
Finally, foundational gameplay mechanics have been completely overhauled alongside these more visual-focused upgrades. Character movement directly influences weapon sway and contextual interactions with walls, while a new physical bullet trajectory simulation replaces older random bloom mechanics.
Together with these technical engineering achievements, Modern Warfare 4 stands as one of the more significant series milestones. It refines the experience for long term fans of the franchise - and impressions from the early access period suggest the campaign at least is one of the series' best in recent memory. We'll have more to say on Modern Warfare 4 to come, including the Switch 2 edition, but for now the outlook on the game's tech is promising to say the least.

EVERETT, Wash.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 22, 2026--
Helion, a Washington-based fusion energy company, announced today it has signed a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce to receive up to $175 million in funding through the CHIPS Research and Development Office to conduct R&D critical for the development and manufacturing of next-generation semiconductor technologies for commercial fusion energy. The expected federal award will be accompanied by $50 million in additional private investment and will support new semiconductor research, manufacturing, and advanced-packaging capabilities in the U.S.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261021509882/en/
Semiconductors used in Helion's pulsed power fusion systems at Helion's headquarters in Everett, Washington.
“Building fusion power plants at scale requires us to accelerate the development of technologies like semiconductors that are critical to making fusion possible,” said David Kirtley, CEO of Helion. “This award combined with additional private investment, totaling $225 million, will allow Helion to develop and manufacture advanced semiconductors here in the United States that deliver the efficiency, reliability, and performance our systems require. It’s an important investment in both America’s semiconductor manufacturing base and the future of commercial fusion.”
Helion’s fusion systems rely on high-power pulsed electrical systems that must repeatedly and efficiently switch and recover large amounts of energy. Semiconductors that perform at the levels the company requires are currently only available from overseas manufacturers. The CHIPS Act Award will support R&D for the U.S. development and transition to manufacturing of Helion's next-generation, high-voltage semiconductors, designed to deliver higher efficiency, longer operating lifetime, and more efficient cooling. Developing these technologies domestically will improve reliability, reduce costs, and remove global supply-chain constraints and risks as Helion moves toward commercial deployment.
“The Trump Administration is accelerating American semiconductor innovation to enhance our domestic energy and power resources,” said Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick. “This investment expands domestic research, secures critical supply chains, and creates high-paying American jobs.”
More than $100 million will support next-generation semiconductor and advanced packaging research and development in Everett, Washington and bring over 100 jobs and substantial power module manufacturing capability to Washington state. The work will also advance new semiconductor packaging capabilities designed to integrate multiple semiconductor devices into efficient, mass-deployable packages.
In addition, approximately $80 million will support R&D for next-generation semiconductor tooling, design, and process development in collaboration with an industry partner in Burlington, Vermont, further strengthening the domestic supply chain for technologies Helion needs to manufacture fusion power plants at scale.
The remaining funds will support R&D for additional enhancements to semiconductor packaging and manufacturing automation.
“This CHIPS R&D award will support innovation in next-generation semiconductor power modules and devices critical to advancing fusion energy,” said Bill Frauenhofer, Executive Director of Semiconductor Investment and Innovation at the Department of Commerce. “Accelerating this R&D domestically will support breakthroughs in America’s ability to convert and deliver power to critical applications in defense, grid transmission, and advanced energy generation.”
Delivering American-made fusion energy to the grid could fundamentally change U.S. strategy from managing energy scarcity to harnessing clean energy abundance, unlocking new industries, strengthening national security, and improving quality of life for all Americans.

Separately, upon entering into a definitive award agreement, to enhance the return for the U.S. taxpayer, the U.S. Department of Commerce would receive a $175 million non-voting interest in Helion based on its most recent Series G preferred stock valuation as a payment for entering into the Award.
The CHIPS Act Award announcement adds to a year filled with significant milestones achieved by Helion, including a $500 million Series G investment round, becoming the first private fusion energy company to demonstrate deuterium-tritium (D-T) fusion and achieve plasma temperatures of 150 million degrees Celsius, as well as ongoing momentum behind Orion, the company’s first fusion power plant.

Helion is a fusion energy company focused on generating zero-carbon electricity from fusion. Its mission is to build the world’s first fusion power plant, enabling a future with unlimited clean electricity. articles.title: TSMC Looks to Replace Chinese Rare-Earth Components in Equipment Used to Make AI Chips - Coinpaper
articles.summary: TSMC Looks to Replace Chinese Rare-Earth Components in Equipment Used to Make AI Chips  Coinpaper
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways
- TSMC explores rare-earth-free motors for semiconductor manufacturing equipment
- China's export restrictions expose another AI chip vulnerability
- Taiwan plans domestic rare-earth production within three years
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) is exploring ways to remove rare-earth components from factory equipment, seeking to reduce its exposure to Chinese export controls that could disrupt production of advanced chips used by Nvidia, Apple and other technology companies.
The initiative, reported by Reuters on October 22, focuses on motors powering automated machinery inside semiconductor manufacturing facilities.
Three industry executives familiar with the discussions said TSMC has approached equipment suppliers about alternatives that do not require rare-earth magnets.
The effort remains preliminary, and the company has not introduced the technology across its manufacturing network.
TSMC Explores Rare-Earth-Free Motors as China Tightens Export Controls
Rare-earth magnets play an important role in industrial motors, particularly where equipment requires precise movement, efficiency and compact designs.
Inside semiconductor factories, automated machinery moves silicon wafers and other components through carefully controlled manufacturing processes.
A shortage of specialized motors or replacement components could therefore complicate equipment maintenance, factory expansion or production schedules.
According to Reuters, TSMC is surveying suppliers about the feasibility of replacing rare-earth-dependent motors in factory automation systems.
The discussions come as equipment manufacturers already face pressure to expand production. Dutch semiconductor supplier ASML recently outlined plans to produce more than 110 EUV machines annually by 2028.
China introduced export controls on selected rare-earth materials, magnets and related technologies in 2025, requiring licenses for certain international shipments.
These restrictions have created uncertainty for manufacturers that depend on specialized components, even when their immediate suppliers operate outside China.
However, Reuters did not establish that TSMC is currently experiencing a shortage or that its manufacturing output has been affected.
Why China's Rare-Earth Restrictions Matter for Nvidia and AMD
TSMC manufactures advanced processors for major technology companies, including Nvidia and AMD, making its production capacity critical to the artificial intelligence industry.
The company recently projected fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion as demand for advanced computing continues expanding.
Meanwhile, AMD has outlined substantial Asian supply-chain investments, reflecting the industry's efforts to secure components and manufacturing capacity years in advance.
Rare-earth availability introduces a different risk.
Rather than affecting the design of AI processors directly, restrictions could complicate the supply of equipment needed to manufacture them.
Developing alternative motors could reduce some dependencies, but replacement systems would need to satisfy semiconductor factories' demanding performance and reliability requirements.
Such changes could also require additional testing and modifications to existing manufacturing equipment.
TSMC has not disclosed the expected cost of any transition or a timetable for deployment.
Taiwan Plans Rare-Earth Production as TSMC Expands Globally
Taiwan is separately working to strengthen domestic rare-earth capabilities.
In February, Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin said the government would support the Industrial Technology Research Institute in developing a pilot production line within three years.
The project aims to establish capacity that could eventually satisfy approximately 50% of Taiwan's domestic rare-earth demand.
US officials have also expressed interest in cooperating with Taiwan to diversify critical-mineral supply chains and expand processing capacity.
The effort complements TSMC's broader Arizona factory expansion, although building semiconductor plants overseas does not automatically eliminate dependence on internationally sourced equipment.
China's mineral export policies have also attracted investor interest in alternative producers, including USA Rare Earth, which is developing domestic mining and magnet manufacturing capacity.
Meanwhile, semiconductor stocks have faced renewed selling pressure despite strong demand for AI infrastructure.

articles.summary: TSMC Seeks Chipmaking Equipment Without Chinese Rare-Earth Magnets  news.lavx.hu
articles.full_text:
TSMC is asking suppliers to build factory automation motors that avoid rare-earth magnets as Beijing's export controls tighten. The move aims to protect production at its automated fabs from supply disruptions.
TSMC is asking equipment suppliers to provide factory automation machinery equipped with motors that avoid rare-earth materials, according to a Reuters report on Oct. 22 citing people familiar with the matter. The world's largest contract chip manufacturer wants to cut dependence on China-dominated supply chains and protect its automated fabs from export-control disruptions.
The company supplies Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom, Qualcomm, and numerous other tech and automotive clients. Its enormous semiconductor fabrication plants rely on electric motors with powerful permanent magnets made from neodymium, dysprosium, and terbium.
The U.S. Geological Survey estimates China accounts for roughly 70% of global rare-earth mining. The International Energy Agency says China controls around 90% of refining and approximately 95% of finished permanent magnets in TSMC's machines.
In April 2025, Beijing placed seven medium and heavy rare earths and their magnets under export controls, requiring case-by-case licenses. Manufacturers in the U.S., Europe, and Asia lost access to shipments, including TSMC. On Oct. 9, 2025, China expanded the controls to include five additional rare earths, processing technology and equipment, and products manufactured outside the country that contain more than 0.1% Chinese-origin rare earths or are made using Chinese processing technology. Beijing suspended the expansion for one year until Nov. 10, 2026, then extended the suspension for an additional 90 days.
TSMC's moves aim to reduce the risk that these controls will hinder production at its factories. Even with other raw materials secured, shortages of specialized motor components could complicate maintenance, repair, or expansion of production equipment.
Several technological approaches allow motors to avoid rare-earth magnets. Conventional induction motors generate torque using electromagnetic induction rather than permanent magnets. Switched-reluctance motors offer another option. Some permanent-magnet motors can use ferrite magnets instead of rare-earth varieties. Each approach carries trade-offs in efficiency, size, power density, precision, and control requirements.
Meanwhile, the rest of the world is building rare-earth supply chains outside China. Taiwan is pursuing domestic production capabilities in collaboration with the United States. The Industrial Technology Research Institute aims to establish a pilot production line within three years that could supply about 50% of Taiwan's domestic rare-earth demand. The U.S. is working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity, and build more resilient supply chains, according to the report.
In February 2026, the Trump administration announced plans to create a $12 billion critical minerals stockpile to offset supply chain risks from China.

Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Semiconductor Diffusion Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global semiconductor diffusion equipment market is entering a structurally significant phase as chipmakers ramp investments in leading-edge logic and memory capacity. Diffusion equipment, which includes batch furnaces and related systems for dopant introduction and thermal processing, sits on the critical path of every wafer fab. Demand is being pulled forward by the transition to sub-3nm gate-all-around logic and 200-plus-layer 3D NAND, where precise thermal budgets and contamination control become non-negotiable.
At the same time, national semiconductor self-sufficiency programs across the US, Europe, Japan, and India are creating new fab clusters, each requiring localized qualification and support infrastructure. The supply landscape remains concentrated among a handful of global OEMs, protected by deep process integration IP and high switching costs. Pricing power is shifting toward service and upgrades, with recurring revenue streams often exceeding initial tool cost.
This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, end-use sectors, regional dynamics, competitive positioning, and the qualification burden that shapes supplier selection. It is designed for equipment manufacturers, subsystem suppliers, investors, and strategic entrants seeking a clear view of where value pools are forming and how procurement logic is evolving.
The baseline scenario for the global semiconductor diffusion equipment market points to steady expansion through 2035, supported by the inexorable push toward advanced process nodes and the geographic diversification of fab capacity. The market is expected to register a CAGR of approximately 6.5% over the forecast period, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to around 185 by 2035. This growth is not linear; it will be punctuated by capex cycles tied to leading-edge foundry and memory investments, but the underlying trajectory remains positive.
The strongest demand pull comes from the transition to gate-all-around logic at 3nm and below, and from 3D NAND stacks exceeding 200 layers, both of which require tighter thermal budget control and higher equipment performance. Diffusion equipment demand is also being supported by the build-out of new fabs in the United States, Europe, Japan, and India, driven by government incentives. However, these new facilities will require extensive qualification cycles, delaying revenue recognition. The aftermarket for refurbished and legacy-node equipment provides a stable counter-cyclical buffer, particularly for automotive and industrial semiconductors.
Supply remains concentrated, with fewer than ten global players controlling the majority of system-level design-ins. Pricing power is concentrated in the service and upgrade layer, where proprietary consumables and process know-how create recurring revenue. Risks include geopolitical export controls, which could fragment the market further, and the potential for a capex digestion phase after the current investment wave. Overall, the outlook is cautiously optimistic, with growth driven by technology transitions and geographic expansion rather than unit-volume increases alone.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Transition to advanced nodes (sub-3nm gate-all-around logic and 200+ layer 3D NAND) requiring tighter thermal budget control and higher equipment performance
- Geographic diversification of semiconductor manufacturing driven by national self-sufficiency policies, creating new fab clusters and parallel qualification pathways
- Rising demand for mature-node semiconductors in automotive, industrial, and IoT applications, sustaining demand for refurbished and legacy diffusion equipment
- Increasing complexity of device architectures, including 3D structures and new materials, which raises the number of diffusion steps per wafer
- Growth in memory capacity investments, particularly DRAM and 3D NAND, as data center and AI workloads drive bit demand
- Government incentives and subsidies for domestic semiconductor production in the US, EU, Japan, and India, accelerating fab construction and equipment orders
Potential Growth Constraints
- High qualification burden and long design-in cycles for new equipment, which slow supplier diversification and delay revenue from new fabs
- Geopolitical export controls and trade restrictions that fragment the market and limit access to certain regions and customers
- Cyclicality of semiconductor capex, with potential digestion phases after periods of heavy investment leading to temporary demand declines
- Technical complexity and high R&D costs required to keep pace with advanced node requirements, posing barriers for smaller suppliers
- Supply chain constraints for critical components such as high-purity quartz and specialty ceramics, which can extend lead times and increase costs
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Semiconductor Foundry (estimated share: 45%)
The foundry segment represents the largest and most technologically demanding end-use sector for semiconductor diffusion equipment. Foundries are ramping production at 5nm, 3nm, and below, where gate-all-around transistor architectures require precise dopant placement and ultra-low contamination levels. Diffusion furnaces are used for well formation, source/drain doping, and thermal annealing steps, with each advanced node adding process steps and tighter specifications. The demand story here is driven by capacity expansions at leading foundries such as TSMC, Samsung Foundry, and Intel Foundry, as well as the emergence of new foundries in the US, Europe, and Japan.
Key demand-side indicators include wafer starts per month at advanced nodes, capital expenditure guidance from major foundries, and the number of new fab projects announced. As foundries transition to gate-all-around and eventually complementary FET architectures, the requirement for diffusion equipment with higher temperature uniformity, faster ramp rates, and reduced particle contamination will intensify. This segment is expected to grow at a CAGR above the market average, supported by the relentless pursuit of Moore's Law and the increasing complexity of logic chips for AI, mobile, and high-performance computing applications. Current trend: Increasing share driven by leading-edge logic investments.
Major trends: Ramp of gate-all-around logic at 3nm and below, Increasing number of diffusion steps per wafer at advanced nodes, Geographic diversification of foundry capacity, Co-development of diffusion processes with foundry customers, and Shift toward single-wafer thermal processing for certain steps.

Memory manufacturers are a critical demand driver for diffusion equipment, particularly as 3D NAND stacks exceed 200 layers and DRAM scaling continues below 1-alpha nodes. In 3D NAND, diffusion processes are essential for creating the alternating dielectric layers and for doping the polysilicon channel, with each additional layer increasing the number of thermal steps and the need for high-throughput batch furnaces. DRAM scaling, meanwhile, requires precise dopant control for buried wordlines and capacitor structures. The demand story is supported by the growing bit demand from data centers, AI accelerators, and consumer devices, which is pushing memory makers to invest in new capacity and technology upgrades.

articles.summary: TSMC is seeking chipmaking equipment that doesn't contain Chinese rare-earth magnets — asks suppliers to provide alternative motors as export controls threaten fab operations  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
TSMC, the world's largest contract chip manufacturer, is seeking alternative machinery without rare-earth components to reduce its dependence on China-dominated materials and avoid disruptions to factory operations caused by the country's export controls. According to a Reuters report on October 22 citing people familiar with the matter, the Taiwanese company has begun approaching its equipment suppliers to explore whether they can provide factory automation equipment equipped with motors that don't require rare-earth materials.
TSMC supplies the extremely powerful Nvidia chips that are facilitating the AI boom. It also manufactures chips for Apple, Broadcom, Qualcomm, and numerous other tech and automotive companies. The company operates enormous, highly automated semiconductor fabrication plants. These factories use industrial machinery that relies on electric motors with powerful permanent magnets made from rare-earth elements such as neodymium, dysprosium, and terbium.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), China accounts for roughly 70% of global rare earth mining. The International Energy Agency (IEA) says China also controls around 90% of refining and approximately 95% of the finished permanent magnets found in TSMC’s machines, giving Beijing a quasi-absolute monopoly over one of the most critical technology supply chains. In April 2025, the country placed seven medium and heavy rare earths and the magnets made from them under export controls, requiring exporters to seek case-by-case approval and export licenses, thereby choking shipments to manufacturers across the U.S., Europe, and Asia, including TSMC.
China expanded the controls on October 9, 2025, to include five additional rare earths, processing technology and equipment, and even products manufactured outside the country that contain more than 0.1% Chinese-origin rare earths, or are made using Chinese processing technology. It later suspended the October expansion for one year, until November 10, 2026. This has now been extended for an additional 90 days.
TSMC’s moves aim to reduce the risk that these controls will hinder production at its factories. Even with all other raw materials and machinery required to manufacture its chips, shortages of specialized motor components could complicate the maintenance, repair, or expansion of its production equipment. Several technological approaches allow motors to avoid rare earth magnets. Conventional induction motors, for example, generate torque using electromagnetic induction rather than permanent magnets. Switched-reluctance motors are another option, while some permanent-magnet motors can use ferrite magnets instead of rare-earth magnets. However, these technologies typically involve different trade-offs in efficiency, size, power density, precision, and control requirements.
Meanwhile, the rest of the world is undertaking the painstaking, drawn-out task of building a rare-earth supply chain outside China. Taiwan is reportedly pursuing domestic rare-earth production capabilities in collaboration with the United States, with both countries confirming their intent to reduce reliance on Chinese rare-earth and critical-mineral supply chains.
Taiwan's government is supporting the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) in establishing a pilot production line within three years that could supply about 50% of Taiwan's domestic rare-earth demand. Meanwhile, the U.S. is “working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity and build more resilient supply chains,” according to the report. In February 2026, the Trump administration announced plans to create a $12 billion critical minerals stockpile to offset supply chain risks from China.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) is exploring alternatives to rare-earth components used in its factory equipment as concerns grow that China’s export restrictions could disrupt production of the advanced semiconductors powering artificial intelligence, smartphones, data centers and defense systems.
The world’s largest contract chipmaker has surveyed suppliers about replacing motors containing rare-earth materials with alternatives in factory-automation equipment, three industry executives briefed on the company’s plans told Reuters. The initiative, reported for the first time, is driven partly by concerns that Beijing’s restrictions could interrupt supplies of specialized components required to keep highly automated semiconductor plants running.
The discussions remain at an early stage and have not yet resulted in a broad deployment of rare-earth-free equipment, two people familiar with the matter said. TSMC declined to comment.

The initiative underpins a less visible vulnerability in the global semiconductor industry. While attention often centers on access to advanced chipmaking technology, manufacturing capacity also depends on a complex network of industrial components and materials that can be difficult to replace quickly.
Rare-earth magnets are used in motors that power moving parts in industrial machinery, including equipment deployed in automated factories. A shortage of specialized motors or related components could create maintenance problems, delay equipment installations, or disrupt production if manufacturers cannot secure suitable replacements.
Such risks for TSMC come with implications that go far beyond Taiwan. The company manufactures advanced chips used across the global technology industry, including processors supporting AI systems and data-center infrastructure. Any prolonged interruption to its operations could affect customers that depend on reliable supplies of high-performance semiconductors.
China’s position in rare-earth supply chains has therefore become a potential source of operational risk for semiconductor manufacturers, even when the materials in question are not direct ingredients in the chips themselves.
Beijing last year placed certain rare-earth materials, magnets and related processing technologies under export controls, requiring licenses for covered exports. The measures have increased concerns among manufacturers that depend on specialized components sourced through Chinese supply chains.
Rare earths are a group of 17 metallic elements used in a range of industrial applications, including permanent magnets, electric motors, electronics and defense equipment. Their importance comes not simply from their availability in the Earth’s crust but from the difficulty of developing competitive alternatives and establishing the processing capacity needed to produce materials at scale.
For semiconductor manufacturers, the concern is the potential for disruption at a point where replacement options may be limited. Chip fabrication plants operate with tightly controlled processes and expensive equipment that must maintain high levels of reliability. A component shortage can become a production risk if equipment cannot be repaired, replaced, or commissioned on schedule.
TSMC’s supplier survey suggests the company is assessing that risk before a disruption occurs. Investigating rare-earth-free motors could give the chipmaker more options if export licensing delays or supply restrictions make existing components harder to obtain.
However, replacing rare-earth-based components in industrial equipment is not necessarily straightforward. Alternative motor designs must meet the performance, precision, reliability, and operating requirements of semiconductor manufacturing. Suppliers may also need to qualify new equipment and demonstrate that it can function consistently in demanding production environments.
The early stage of TSMC’s discussions indicates that reducing dependence on rare-earth components is likely to be a gradual engineering and supply-chain exercise rather than an immediate switch.
The episode also demonstrates how export controls can influence industrial decisions even before they produce a confirmed shortage. The possibility that critical components may become harder to obtain can encourage manufacturers to diversify suppliers, redesign equipment, and hold additional inventories, potentially increasing costs across the supply chain.
Taiwan and The US Pursue Alternative Supply Chains
TSMC’s initiative comes as Taiwan and the United States seek to reduce their reliance on Chinese sources of rare earths and other critical minerals.
In June, Raymond F. Greene, director of the American Institute in Taiwan, Washington’s de facto embassy on the island, said the United States was working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity and strengthen supply-chain resilience.
Taiwan has also outlined plans to develop domestic rare-earth capabilities. In February, Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin said the government would support the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI), a domestic research organization, in developing rare-earth technologies.
The plan envisages establishing a pilot production line within three years that could meet an estimated 50% of Taiwan’s domestic demand, according to Kung. The target points to an effort to build local capabilities, although a pilot line would not by itself establish that Taiwan could replace Chinese supplies across all rare-earth materials and industrial applications.
ITRI said it was working with the Department of Industrial Technology at Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs to plan a rare-earth project but provided no further details.
US officials have also shown interest in ITRI’s work and held discussions with the institute on diversifying critical-mineral supply chains, according to a person at a US-based think tank familiar with the talks. The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
These efforts reflect the growing overlap between industrial policy and technology security. Governments are increasingly concerned that concentrated control over materials and processing capabilities could give suppliers leverage over industries considered economically or strategically important.
The challenge impacts Taiwan significantly because its semiconductor industry depends on uninterrupted access to specialized equipment, components, and materials from international suppliers. Developing domestic alternatives could reduce exposure to external supply shocks, but establishing viable production capacity requires investment, technical expertise and time.
The United States faces a similar challenge in trying to diversify supply chains while maintaining access to materials needed for electronics, advanced manufacturing and defense. Building alternative sources involves more than identifying new mines; processing, refining, magnet production, and qualification of finished components must also be developed.
Nevertheless, TSMC’s exploration of rare-earth-free equipment shows that the semiconductor supply chain extends well beyond the fabrication process itself. The industry’s resilience is based on access to the motors, machinery, materials, and specialized parts that allow chipmaking facilities to operate continuously.
The risk is not that China’s export controls have already halted TSMC’s production. The reported supplier discussions instead indicate that the company is examining potential vulnerabilities and evaluating alternatives before any disruption materializes.
Replacing components across a semiconductor factory can be costly and technically demanding. This means manufacturers must weigh the expense of redesigning equipment against the potential consequences of relying on suppliers exposed to geopolitical restrictions.
The broader challenge, however, lies in the ability of Taiwan and its international partners to build alternative supply chains quickly enough to reduce concentrated dependencies without creating new bottlenecks or substantially increasing manufacturing costs.

Elon Musk is exploring a historic merger between Tesla and SpaceX that could create a technology giant worth approximately $3.5 trillion, combining electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, robotics, satellite communications and space exploration under one corporate structure.
During SpaceX's October 20 earnings call, Musk confirmed that both companies had established special committees of independent directors to evaluate a potential transaction. He expressed support for combining the businesses but emphasized that no agreement had been reached.
The discussions represent a significant shift from earlier speculation surrounding a possible SpaceX partnership with Tesla. What once appeared to be overlapping technology projects could become one of the largest corporate combinations ever contemplated.
A $3.4 Trillion Merger Would Reshape Musk's Empire
SpaceX carried a market capitalization of approximately $1.95 trillion on October 20, while Tesla was valued at roughly $1.48 trillion. Together, the companies represented about $3.43 trillion in market value before accounting for merger terms, ownership adjustments or market movements.
SpaceX's June stock market debut transformed the aerospace company into a publicly traded technology giant. Its rapid expansion into artificial intelligence has further complicated the distinction between Musk's different businesses.
The company's third-quarter revenue reached $14.6 billion, up 161% year over year, with net income of $4.4 billion. Its Super Intelligence division contributed approximately $7.6 billion, making AI computing a larger revenue source than Starlink's connectivity operations.
Why Tesla and SpaceX Could Be Worth More Together
The potential merger reflects growing technological overlap between the companies. Tesla develops energy storage systems, autonomous driving technology, AI chips and humanoid robots, while SpaceX operates satellite networks, launch systems and increasingly substantial computing infrastructure.
SpaceX previously absorbed xAI, bringing its AI development ambitions closer to its orbital computing plans. Meanwhile, Tesla's hardware capabilities could potentially support future data-center and robotics projects across the combined organization.
Financing provides another possible motivation. SpaceX has reportedly pursued additional borrowing to purchase Nvidia chips, underscoring the enormous capital requirements of its expanding AI operations.
Combining businesses would not automatically reduce those costs, but it could allow coordinated investment decisions and closer integration of technologies already being developed across Musk's companies.
Tesla Shareholders Could Decide the Merger's Future
Despite Musk's support, completing the transaction would be considerably more complicated than simply combining two companies under his leadership.
Musk has substantial control over SpaceX but a smaller ownership position in Tesla. He said Tesla shareholder approval would represent a significant obstacle, while independent committees must first examine whether a transaction benefits each company's investors.
Potential regulatory concerns also remain, particularly because SpaceX has sensitive U.S. government and military relationships while Tesla maintains extensive manufacturing and commercial operations in China.
The discussions come as SpaceX expands beyond satellites through Starlink's connectivity business, while Tesla increasingly positions itself around autonomy, robotics and energy.

articles.summary: Chinese tech giants place over $35bn in Nvidia chip orders  Big News Network.com
articles.full_text:
BEIJING, China: ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have placed orders worth more than US$35 billion for Nvidia's new export-compliant graphics cards as Chinese technology companies scramble for AI computing power amid U.S. restrictions on more advanced chips.
The three Chinese technology giants have ordered more than three million RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards, according to two people familiar with the matter. The cards cost about $11,400 each.
Nvidia has told customers and partners it cannot guarantee it can fill orders because demand from Chinese tech companies far exceeds planned production, the two sources and a third person familiar with the matter said.
The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation chip designed for powerful professional computers rather than the large data-center clusters that use Nvidia's most advanced AI processors. However, it is among the most powerful Nvidia chips still available to Chinese buyers.
Nvidia's Blackwell-based B300 data-center chip cannot be sold to Chinese buyers under U.S. export controls, while exports of its Hopper-based H200 are reviewed on a case-by-case basis and subject to licensing conditions.
One source said Nvidia told partners they might receive only 5 percent to 10 percent of the quantities requested. Another said the company had indicated it could produce no more than three million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally in 2027.
Total orders from customers in China have exceeded six million cards, two of the sources said.
The demand underscores Chinese companies' continued appetite for Nvidia hardware despite U.S. restrictions. Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang has said the curbs reduced the company's share of China's AI data-center chip market from near-monopoly to effectively nothing.
Washington's restrictions have pushed Chinese companies toward domestic suppliers, while Beijing has encouraged the use of homegrown chips. Huawei has gained market share, although Chinese chipmakers have generally struggled to match leading U.S. products.
An Nvidia spokesperson said Chinese producers of workstation chips and cards have experienced "unprecedented growth since 2022," when the restrictions were first imposed.
"U.S. firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly a half a decade ago, and China's own limit on US imports," the spokesperson said.
ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment.
Chinese companies are seeking to use the RTX PRO 5500 primarily for AI inference, or running trained models to generate chatbot responses, according to the three sources.
Nvidia is expected to devote much of its capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co from 2027 to Rubin, its next-generation platform for large-scale data centers, rather than products such as the RTX PRO 5500, two sources said.
Nvidia has told customers to expect early samples of the RTX PRO 5500 in December, with commercial deliveries beginning in the first quarter of 2027, they added.

articles.title: Israel’s military wants hundreds of satellites and a new generation of war robots - CTech
articles.summary: Israel’s military wants hundreds of satellites and a new generation of war robots  CTech
articles.full_text:
Israel’s military wants hundreds of satellites and a new generation of war robots
The IDF is expanding its ambitions in space and autonomous warfare, aiming to improve intelligence coverage and reduce risks to troops. The plans could generate billions of shekels in business for defense contractors, but the funding remains uncertain as the military seeks a major budget increase.
Last week, the Ministry of Finance had to impose an urgent, across-the-board budget cut at the last minute to secure funding for the procurement of 12 Apache helicopters from the United States. At the same time, the IDF is embarking on an ambitious expansion of its military capabilities in space and robotics, with plans that could require billions of shekels in additional investment.
The military’s ambitions include a dramatic expansion of Israel’s intelligence satellite fleet, potentially to several dozen satellites within a few years and eventually hundreds, alongside the accelerated development of capabilities for warfare in space. The IDF has now moved to establish dedicated Space and Robotics divisions, formalizing two areas it sees as increasingly important to future combat operations.
The scale of the planned investment in space remains classified, as do many details of the broader program. The new Space Division will operate under the IDF Planning Directorate and will delegate responsibilities across several military bodies, primarily the Air Force, the Intelligence Directorate and the C4I Directorate, which oversees communications and information systems.
The move was reflected in a recent round of senior appointments by Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir. Brig. Gen. “S.” was selected to head the new Space Division, while two additional officers were appointed to lead departments within it and are set to be promoted to colonel. The division is part of the IDF’s multiyear Hoshen plan, which is intended to shape the military’s capabilities for the coming years. The long-term ambition is to turn space into a distinct military domain, with dedicated operational responsibilities and expertise.
At the heart of the initiative is a planned constellation of satellites designed to provide more persistent intelligence coverage of multiple regions around the world. Israel’s current reconnaissance satellites orbit at an altitude of roughly 450 kilometers, completing a full orbit approximately every 90 minutes. A satellite passing over a particular location can observe it for only a few minutes before moving out of range, leaving a gap until its next pass.
The IDF wants to narrow those gaps by deploying a much larger number of satellites, enabling more continuous surveillance of areas of operational interest. The goal is to give commanders a more up-to-date picture of developments on the ground, reducing the risk that significant movements or events go undetected between satellite passes.
The expansion into space is part of a broader technological transformation the IDF is pursuing after more than three years of war. Alongside new intelligence and operational capabilities beyond Earth’s atmosphere, the military is establishing a Robotics Division within the Depth Corps, commanded by Maj. Gen. Dan Goldfus.
The new division is intended to accelerate the development and integration of autonomous systems that can reduce the risks faced by combat personnel. Its remit includes ground-based robotic platforms operating in coordination with drones, unmanned aerial vehicles and other systems for both defensive and offensive missions. Brig. Gen. “Y.” has been selected to command the division.
The ambitions, however, face an immediate obstacle: money. While the IDF intends to finance the new capabilities through its procurement plans for the coming years, Ministry of Finance officials have questioned how the military will pay for the proposed expansion, according to conversations with Calcalist. Major funding decisions will ultimately depend on the government formed after next week’s general election, if a government is formed.
A senior Finance Ministry official highlighted the gap between the military’s ambitions and the resources available to fund them.
“Just last week, we had to implement an urgent, across-the-board budget cut to scrape together a billion shekels to cover a shortfall for the defense establishment to order 12 Apache helicopters, and even that was a struggle,” the official said. “The military is well aware of the complexities of the current budgetary situation. We expect them to tell us where the money for this is supposed to come from, because we certainly don’t know.”
The dispute comes amid a prolonged crisis of trust between the Finance and Defense ministries. Senior defense officials are looking to the next government to resolve the budget impasse and secure additional resources. The defense budget for 2026 already stands at NIS 158 billion, while the Defense Ministry and the IDF are demanding tens of billions of shekels more by the end of the year, potentially pushing the total to an unprecedented NIS 183 billion.
The planned investments could also create significant opportunities for Israel’s defense industry. Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) is likely to be among the main beneficiaries, given its longstanding expertise in satellites, space-based sensors and unmanned systems operating on land, in the air and at sea.
Nearly four decades after launching the first Ofek reconnaissance satellite for Israel’s defense establishment, IAI launched the Ofek 19 radar-imaging satellite from central Israel in September 2025. The satellite was carried into orbit by the Shavit launch vehicle, also developed by IAI, with its engines manufactured by Tomer.
The new satellites under consideration are expected to be smaller than the reconnaissance satellites Israel has traditionally relied on, but deployed in far greater numbers. The approach draws in part on the model popularized by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, whose Starlink constellation comprises thousands of communications satellites providing broadband internet services.
“Some of these concepts are mature, allowing us to move forward rapidly and aggressively, while others still fall into the realm of science fiction, though not for much longer. We are making great strides across several programs,” a senior defense official told Calcalist.
The expected investment is also likely to intensify competition among Israel’s major defense contractors. Rafael has expanded its work on small satellites in recent years, while Elbit Systems is developing specialized payloads carried by satellites for a range of missions.
A senior executive at a defense company expecting to compete for part of the planned spending said the value of the new systems would extend beyond the satellites themselves.
“A large constellation of satellites operating simultaneously will generate a stream of data. This data will be instantly analyzed using AI tools, providing field commanders with an up-to-the-minute situational picture and insights into events within their operational theater, in addition to further capabilities yet to come,” the executive told Calcalist.
The defense establishment has disclosed little about its plans for space warfare, leaving the precise capabilities under development largely unknown. The ambitions extend beyond using satellites to gather intelligence, but officials have offered few details about what future offensive or defensive systems might look like.
“We aren’t quite at the point where a precise laser beam fired from a satellite 500 kilometers up can destroy a ground target, but there are some very interesting things in the pipeline,” a senior defense official said.
As military reliance on space grows, so does the need to protect satellites against attacks and disruption. TSG, a subsidiary of IAI and the Formula Group, intends to offer the IDF systems designed to protect space-based assets against cyberattacks, anti-satellite weapons and even collisions with space debris.
“Damage to space-based assets could severely disrupt a nation’s functional continuity. Consequently, increasing efforts to protect these assets has become a central component of strategic planning,” Gilad Sharoni, TSG’s vice president of research and development, said on Wednesday.
The new Robotics Division is also expected to create opportunities for Israeli defense-tech companies seeking a share of the military’s procurement spending. The market has expanded as the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have accelerated demand for drones, autonomous platforms and other unmanned systems.
The American company Ondas has acquired more than 20 companies, most of them Israeli, specializing in drones and autonomous systems. It recently secured a place in the IDF’s Digital Bat (Atalef Digitali) program for tactical attack drones, joining companies including Kela and Aitan.
Goldfus is expected to visit several defense companies working on new robotic systems in the coming weeks, including IAI-Elta’s Land Systems division. Elbit Systems is also preparing for increased demand, having established FUSE, a defense-tech arm focused on ground robotics and drones. The initiative is intended to strengthen Elbit’s position as it competes with a growing number of younger companies entering the sector.
For Israel’s defense industry, the IDF’s plans could open a new wave of procurement opportunities in space, robotics and autonomous warfare. But with the military already seeking a substantial increase in its budget and the Finance Ministry struggling to fund existing commitments, the central question is whether the government can turn these ambitions into funded programs.

articles.title: SpaceX Q3 2026: First-Ever Profit of $4.4 Billion as AI Revenue Overtakes Starlink - Techi
articles.summary: SpaceX Q3 2026: First-Ever Profit of $4.4 Billion as AI Revenue Overtakes Starlink  Techi
articles.full_text:
SpaceX (Nasdaq: SPCX) reported its first quarterly profit as a public company on Tuesday, posting net income of $4.4 billion for the third quarter as revenue rose 161% to $14.6 billion, well above the $12.7 billion analysts expected, with its Super Intelligence segment overtaking Starlink's parent business to become the company's largest.
The stock rose 7.8% on Wednesday to close at $159.31, its first session after the release. Diluted earnings per share were $0.35, against consensus expectations of about $0.14. Adjusted EBITDA reached $8.8 billion, up 306% from a year earlier. TECHi's preview of the report said the quarter would be judged against the bar set in Q2, because SpaceX gives no guidance: a full quarter of its Cursor acquisition, a full quarter of interest on its $25 billion bond, and an AI capital bill that had already doubled once. On the measures the preview set, SpaceX cleared the bar — and the same release shows what the clearance cost.
- First profitNet income of $4.4 billion versus a $1.1 billion loss a year earlier; diluted EPS of $0.35 against expectations of about $0.14.
- AI is the majoritySuper Intelligence revenue of $7.56 billion was 51.9% of the total, up from 15% a year ago, and the segment posted its first operating profit.
- The spending billCapital expenditure of $19.6 billion equalled 134% of quarterly revenue; SI alone spent $16.4 billion, 2.2 times its own revenue.
- Profit qualityAbout 37% of net income came from below the operating line — interest income, a $1.03 billion other-income line and a tax benefit — and nine-month free cash flow was about −$35.0 billion (TECHi calculation).
- Starlink13.6 million consumer subscribers, up 1.6 million in the quarter; consumer ARPU of $69 was down from $83 a year earlier.
The quarter against the bar Q2 set
Revenue of $14.575 billion was up 87% from Q2's $7.814 billion in a single quarter. Income from operations swung to $2.791 billion from a $143 million loss in Q2 and a $273 million loss a year earlier. The net income figure compares with a net loss of $1.054 billion in the third quarter of 2025; for the nine months to September 30, SpaceX remains $413 million in the red, because the first half's losses have not yet been fully earned back.
Segment detail from the release: Super Intelligence revenue $7.560 billion (Q2: $2.561 billion), Connectivity $5.248 billion (Q2: $4.291 billion), Space $1.767 billion (Q2: $962 million). Every segment beat the consensus figures circulating before the report, with total revenue about 15% above the $12.72 billion LSEG consensus.
| SpaceX results: Q3 2026 vs Q2 2026 vs Q3 2025 |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Metric | Q3 2026 | Q2 2026 | Q3 2025 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $14.58B | $7.81B | $5.58B | 
| Operating income (loss) | $2.79B | −$0.14B | −$0.27B | 
| Adjusted EBITDA | $8.81B | $3.54B | $2.17B | 
| Capital expenditure | $19.59B | $18.37B | $6.88B | 
| Super Intelligence revenue | $7.56B | $2.56B | $0.81B | 
Where the $4.4 billion came from
The operating business earned $2.791 billion of the $4.404 billion net income — about 63%. TECHi's calculation from the statements in the release shows the remaining $1.613 billion, roughly 37%, arrived below the operating line: $873 million of interest income, earned largely on the cash pile from June's IPO; $1.025 billion of other income, net, of which $561 million is identified as related-party; less $675 million of interest expense, of which $351 million is related-party; plus a $390 million income-tax benefit that added to, rather than reduced, the result.
None of that makes the profit artificial — interest income on a $51.3 billion cash balance is real money, and the operating swing from a $143 million loss to a $2.791 billion profit in one quarter is the genuine inflection. But the composition matters for what repeats. The related-party share of both the interest bill and the other-income line runs through the wider Musk ecosystem of companies, and the release does not break out what the $561 million related-party gain consists of. That detail, if it comes, will arrive in the quarterly 10-Q rather than the earnings release.
Super Intelligence is now the company
A year ago the segment SpaceX then called Artificial Intelligence produced $813 million, 15% of revenue. In Q2 it produced $2.561 billion, 33%. In Q3, renamed Super Intelligence, it produced $7.560 billion — 51.9% of everything SpaceX sold, more than Connectivity and Space combined. TECHi's calculation: $5.0 billion of the $6.8 billion of revenue SpaceX added versus Q2 came from SI alone, driven, the company says, by new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor — completed in August and consolidated for a full quarter for the first time — and adoption of its SI models and software, including Grok Bot.
SI also posted its first operating profit: $431 million, against a $1.257 billion operating loss in Q2 and a $1.722 billion loss a year earlier. Its operating margin, though, was 5.7%, against 45.1% for Connectivity — the satellite business remains far more profitable per dollar of revenue. And SI's expansion is capital-hungry in a way Starlink never was: the segment's capital expenditure was $16.444 billion in the quarter, 2.2 times its own revenue and 84% of the company total. Nameplate compute reached 1.7 gigawatts at September 30, up from 1.4 GW at June 30 and 0.6 GW a year earlier.
Starlink keeps compounding — at thinner prices
Connectivity revenue rose 69% year over year to $5.248 billion, with operating income up 99% to $2.367 billion. Starlink consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million at September 30, up 1.6 million in the quarter and from 7.2 million a year earlier; enterprise and government revenue within the segment was $2.127 billion. The trade-off is price: consumer ARPU was $69 a month, up from $66 in Q2 but down from $83 a year ago, as growth comes from cheaper plans and markets.
The Space segment, meanwhile, nearly broke even — an operating loss of just $7 million on $1.767 billion of revenue, against a $542 million loss in Q2. SpaceX flew 35 launches in the quarter (12 customer, 23 internal) and completed its first revenue-generating Starship mission, delivering 26 Starlink V3 satellites — about ten times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch, the company says.
The cash equation underneath
Total capital expenditure was $19.593 billion in the quarter, 134% of revenue. Across the nine months, SpaceX generated $13.097 billion of operating cash flow and spent $48.069 billion on property, plant and equipment — free cash flow of roughly negative $35.0 billion, by TECHi's calculation. The funding is not in question this year: cash and equivalents stood at $51.294 billion at September 30, and the company also bought $46.8 billion of marketable securities during the nine months, parking IPO proceeds. The open question is duration: at Q3's pace of spending, even a $51 billion cash balance plus securities is a runway measured in quarters, which makes SI's revenue durability — how much of Q3's cloud-agreement surge is recurring — the number that decides the story in Q4.
The merger question
On Tuesday's earnings call, Elon Musk said the boards of SpaceX and Tesla have formed committees to discuss a merger of the two companies, according to reports of the call, and argued there is "a lot of merit" in combining them. Wedbush's Dan Ives was reported estimating an 80% to 90% chance of a merger by the end of 2027. Nothing about a transaction is in the earnings release, and the two companies already transact with each other — the related-party interest and income lines above are part of that existing web — so investors should treat the committee news as a direction of travel, not a deal.
What to watch
Three things decide whether Q3 was an inflection or a spike. First, the 10-Q: it should detail the related-party other income, the digital-asset position ($1.573 billion at September 30, with a $64 million unrealized loss over nine months) and any colour on how much SI revenue is contracted versus one-off. Second, Q4 SI revenue: Q3 included the first full quarter of Cursor and the start of new cloud agreements; a flat or falling SI line would reframe this quarter as a step-change in level rather than in growth rate. Third, the spending line: capex has risen from $6.9 billion a year ago to $19.6 billion, and the market is now capitalising the company above $2 trillion on the assumption that the SI build-out converts to durable, higher-margin revenue before the cash pile thins.

A powerful gene-editing technique has been used to edit DNA directly in a person’s body — the first known instance of such a treatment.
The milestone treatment is part of a clinical trial of prime editing, a technique that can alter DNA with more precision than standard CRISPR–Cas9 methods can. In this case, prime editing was used to treat a condition called Wilson disease by rewriting DNA in liver cells, to erase a mutation that prevents them from eliminating excess copper.
Prime Medicine, a biotechnology company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, announced that it had treated the first person in its trial earlier this month. It expects to announce the first results from the study next year.
“I never dreamed that in my lifetime I would see this applied to my rare disease,” says Rhonda Rowland, president of the Wilson Disease Association in Atlanta, Georgia. “It’s going to be a really exciting year.”
In launching the trial, Prime Medicine joins a host of companies aiming to engineer cells directly in the body, rather than using the standard method of extracting a person’s cells, editing their DNA in a laboratory and then reinjecting the altered cells. Rewriting DNA in the body, or in vivo, is appealing because manufacturing and administering the treatment might be much cheaper and faster than making a bespoke therapy for each person from their own cells.
But in vivo approaches have their own challenges, says Krishanu Saha, a biomedical engineer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “It depends on what types of risks you’re willing to accept,” he says.
Prime time
Wilson disease is caused by mutations in a gene called ATP7B, which encodes a protein that transports excess copper out of the liver. If left untreated, the resulting build-up of copper can cause liver and nerve damage, as well as neurological disorders.
People with Wilson disease are eager for a one-and-done treatment for their condition, says Rowland, rather than the current, complicated regimen of copper-clearing molecules and other medicines. And gene editing could, in theory, provide a lasting solution by correcting the faulty ATP7B gene.
So far, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved only one gene-editing therapy, called Casgevy, which is used to treat two inherited blood disorders. Casgevy relies on CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing, which is often used to disable genes rather than to rewrite their sequences.
Another form of gene editing, called base editing, can rewrite individual DNA letters, but cannot make the particular corrections needed to fix the most common ATP7B mutations. That left prime editing, a more complex and versatile system that can insert, delete and rewrite segments of DNA. In another clinical trial, Prime Medicine used the technique to treat two people with a rare immune disorder, by rewriting DNA in each participant’s blood stem cells outside of the body and then injecting them back in.
So far, no gene-editing therapies have been approved for use in vivo. But the FDA is expected to issue a decision early next year about an in vivo CRISPR–Cas9 therapy for a condition called hereditary angioedema, which causes severe swelling.

A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation. Data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance must converge to work as one. About the speaker







Jing Wang, Principal, Center for AI and Insights, Vanguard







Jing Wang leads Vanguard’s Center for AI & Insights (CAI), advancing the firm’s AI, machine learning, generative AI, and behavioral science capabilities. Her team drives enterprise-wide innovation, research, and delivery, enabling Vanguard to translate emerging technologies into trusted solutions that enhance client experiences, improve investor outcomes, and create measurable business value.



Before her current position, Jing served in a range of leadership roles across Vanguard’s Financial Services, Workplace Solutions, International, and Corporate Services divisions. Throughout her tenure, she has led teams and enterprise initiatives that advanced strategic priorities, strengthened client outcomes, and drove business performance across the firm.



She joined Vanguard in 2009 after several years as a Principal at the Boston Consulting Group. Jing earned a B.S. in Physics from the University of Science and Technology of China, a Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania, and an M.B.A. in Finance and Marketing from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania. Jing holds Series 7, 24, and 65 licenses.

articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



How far can we push computing?



On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued. We simply had not built the tools yet.



He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size. But that easy descent has now stalled. Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance.



Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement. 



Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing.



—Volkan Gurses



This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine: The Impossible issue. Subscribe now to read it in full.



It’s also part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series exploring the ideas shaping technology. Read more from the series. 



Three things you should know about permafrost



How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.



The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just helicoptered into Alaska’s forests to report on the fires threatening permafrost and their complicated potential climate effects.



Here are three things I took away from his reporting.



—Casey Crownhart



This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.



Roundtables: a conversation with the creator of AI-designed viruses



Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King offered a preliminary answer by using a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. 



In our latest Roundtables conversation, MIT Technology Review senior AI reporter James O’Donnell spoke with King about his work, being named one of our Innovators Under 35, and new ways of seeing biology. Subscribers can now watch a full recording of the event.



Want to join the next conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 AI has uncovered a decade-old flaw threatening much of the webIt found flaws in PHP, the code behind most websites. (Reuters $)+ Governments are urging website owners to patch PHP or take sites offline. (BBC)+ Exploit attempts jumped from thousands to millions after disclosure. (Axios)+ Now is a good time for doing crime. (MIT Technology Review)



2 Hackers used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on over 400 banksThe AI agents targeted financial institutions in Latin America. (Information $)+ Unvetted AI agents are also accessing US bank accounts.(Axios)+ Barclays says AI is allowing the bank to cut 5,000 jobs. (Guardian)+ AI is making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)



3 The Pentagon has cleared the DHS to test a heat ray weaponIt could be used for crowd control at the southern US border. (CNN)+ It uses invisible energy beams to produce a burning sensation. (Axios)



4 A startup says AI-designed viruses have treated their first patientThe experimental treatment targets drug-resistant E. coli. (NYT $)+ But the company has not published peer-reviewed results. (Futurism)+ AI-designed viruses are already killing bacteria. (MIT Technology Review)



5 Japan hopes to return the first samples from Mars’s moonsIts spacecraft is now on its way to Phobos. (Guardian)+ It aims to reveal whether Mars was once habitable. (Economist $)



6 Meta faces a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandalThe company says it will appeal the New Mexico ruling. (CNBC)+ A Meta share deal has convinced Mark Zuckerberg to stay in California. (WSJ $)+ Until the company remade its stock structure to help him pay it. (NYT $)



7 A new antimatter experiment could open the door to new physicsScientists hope to spot differences between matter and antimatter. (Nature)



8 China’s Unitree is pitching its latest humanoid as a robot bodyguardA promotional clip shows the H2-X disarming attackers. (SCMP)



9 Just Eat has apologised for bizarre AI-generated menu picturesUsers were unimpressed by the bacon in cola and cheese sushi. (BBC)



10 Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do choresHosts are threatening to strike, but guests are celebrating. (Wired $)



Quote of the day



“Now they’ve given everybody a reason not to use Starlink: that Starlink isn’t reliable for national security for anybody but Trump. Maybe he’d turn it off on the United States if he didn’t like policy and he didn’t like the president.”



 —SpaceX investor Ross Gerber tells CNN that Elon Musk’s decision to restrict Ukraine’s Starlink access has made the service a liability for every other government that relies on it.



One more thing







Online harassment is entering its AI era



Scott Shambaugh didn’t think twice when he denied an AI agent’s request to contribute to matplotlib, a software library he helps manage. Then things got weird. 



In the middle of the night, Shambaugh opened his email to discover the agent had retaliated with a blog post. Titled “Gatekeeping in Open Source: The Scott Shambaugh Story,” the post accused him of rejecting the code out of a fear of being supplanted by AI. “He tried to protect his little fiefdom,” the agent wrote. “It’s insecurity, plain and simple.” 



Shambaugh isn’t alone in facing misbehaving agents—and they’re unlikely to stop at harassment. Read the full story.



—Grace Huckins

articles.summary: "Userland" exploit relies on integer overflow found in "SmileBasic" interpreter.
articles.full_text:
A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO."
The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.
Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory.Read full article

articles.summary: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift.
